transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-19 14:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Samira Chen (Redwood AE); Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE); Daniel Park (StratusBank - Head of Platforms); Priya Kapoor (StratusBank - Secops); Ethan Liu (StratusBank - ML Engineer)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand StratusBank's constraints for moving production LLM workloads to dedicated capacity: isolation, throughput (reserved GPUs), burst handling, autoscaling/queueing expectations, security/compliance (SOC2, KMS, audit logs), and timeline for pilot.

Topics:
- Current infra and workloads
- Isolation/tenancy and data controls
- Expected QPS, token volume, and burst patterns
- Latency SLOs vs cost tradeoffs
- Integration requirements (VPC, KMS, SSO)
- Next steps: pricing, security docs, benchmark run

[00:00] Samira Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off - i'm samira from redwood, account lead, and miguel who's our se is with me. can you, daniel, kick us off with a quick intro to what you folks are trying to do?

[00:12] Daniel Park: yeah hi thanks samira, daniel here. we're exploring moving our customer-facing summarization and routing models off the shared hosted api into dedicated capacity, mostly for isolation and predictable throughput. we've got a mix of batch and near-realtime flows; peak bursts during statement cycles and marketing pushes.

[00:28] Priya Kapoor: and security side i'm priya, we'll need to validate encryption at rest/in transit, KMS, and auditability. also data residency for some EU customers.

[00:36] Miguel Alvarez: great - can you give a sense of current traffic shape? avg qps, tokens per request, and burst factors? even rough numbers help us size.

[00:44] Ethan Liu: sure. for the summarization pipeline avg is ~8 qps, typical request 250-600 tokens in, about 150 tokens out. bursts can go to 120 qps for 10-15 minutes during batch runs. batch jobs for overnight processing are larger: 1M tokens/hour.

[01:05] Daniel Park: we care about p95 latency under 300ms for the near-realtime path. if we can get that with dedicated GPUs that's ideal.

[01:12] Samira Chen: okay that's helpful. so two main needs: reserved capacity for consistent throughput and isolation for compliance. a couple questions - are you planning to run on a private network (VPC) or is hosted but dedicated acceptable?

[01:23] Priya Kapoor: we prefer VPC peering or private link. cannot have data flowing through a multi-tenant control plane without being able to prove controls; but we can discuss a private control plane.

[01:34] Miguel Alvarez: technically we support three modes - hosted dedicated (reserved pools but managed network paths), dedicated with VPC peering, and private deployment where control plane is customer-managed. For compliance you'd likely want dedicated with VPC + customer-managed KMS.

[01:47] Daniel Park: when you say dedicated pool what's the SLA on throughput and latency? how deterministic is it relative to say, running your own EC2 clusters?

[01:55] Miguel Alvarez: dedicated pools are reserved GPU capacity with allocation guarantees per commitment tier. latency is primarily a function of model, quantization, and instance family; we publish performance profiles but for exact P95 numbers we do a benchmark run with your prompts. compared to EC2 self-hosting, hosts get kernel-level optimizations, batching, and kv cache that improve tail latency - plus we manage autoscaler and fallbacks.

[02:20] Ethan Liu: curious about burst strategy - if we commit to a base capacity but see spikes, can you burst beyond reserved? how's billing handled?

[02:29] Samira Chen: yes, bursting is supported via a burst pool or on-demand capacity; pricing differs - bursts billed at a premium hourly rate. you can configure burst limits and policies (cost vs latency prioritization). many customers keep a small reserved pool for baseline steady state and allow controlled bursts for spikes.

[02:44] Priya Kapoor: what's the isolation model? will other tenants ever share the same GPU? that's a big red flag for our compliance folks.

[02:52] Miguel Alvarez: for dedicated pools GPUs are reserved to your tenancy - no co-tenancy on the same GPU. Under the hosted-dedicated offering we still handle the control plane but compute is isolated. only in the shared hosted offering would you see multi-tenant GPUs.

[03:05] Daniel Park: ok good. and for the VPC setup, do you support customer-managed encryption keys? we run all secrets through our HSM.

[03:12] Miguel Alvarez: yes, KMS integration supported - we have options for AWS KMS and external HSM via a partner model. we can document key rotation, access logs, and provide the audit trail.

[03:21] Ethan Liu: on the model side - we currently run a finetuned open model. how do upgrades and rollouts work? can we pin model versions and do canary deploys?

[03:29] Samira Chen: absolutely. you can pin to a model version and we support canary rollouts, A/B routing, and automatic fallback to a lower-cost variant if the primary is unhealthy. the console gives per-model latency and cost breakdowns.

[03:41] Daniel Park: what's the onboarding time for dedicated capacity? we have a compliance window and calendar - ideally pilot in 6 weeks. is that feasible?

[03:49] Miguel Alvarez: pilot in 6 weeks is realistic. typical flow: sizing + contract (1-2 weeks), provisioning the reserved pool and VPC peering (1 week), security review and key exchange (1 week), and benchmark/pilot (1-2 weeks). -> we can compress if approvals are faster.

[04:05] Priya Kapoor: during the security review we will ask for SOC 2 report, penetration test summary, and network diagrams. do you have those ready to share?

[04:12] Samira Chen: yes we'll share SOC2, encryption docs, network diagram for VPC peering, and a mapping of audit logs. i'll attach them after the call.

[04:19] Ethan Liu: performance - what kind of instruments do we get for tracing per request? need to tie tokens/cost to our request ids.

[04:26] Miguel Alvarez: we provide per-request tracing hooks and token-level cost breakdowns. you can send a request id in headers and see that reflected in logs. the console also surfaces per-route token counts and the KV cache hit rates.

[04:38] Daniel Park: ok good. what's the minimum commitment size? and can we scale up during the year?

[04:44] Samira Chen: commitment tiers vary by region & instance family. we have monthly and annual reserved plans. scaling up is straightforward - additional reserved capacity can be added and pro-rated. for scaling down we usually recommend term-based contracts to get the reserve discount; otherwise month-to-month reserved is possible at a higher price.

[04:58] Priya Kapoor: auditability question - how long do you retain logs? we need 12 months of audit trails for certain workflows.

[05:05] Miguel Alvarez: we retain operational logs for default retention; extended retention is available as an add-on. we can configure export to your S3 or SIEM for long-term storage.

[05:14] Ethan Liu: one more technical: kv cache warmup - for our summarization we rely on prefix caching between related user sessions. how does the runtime handle warm cache after autoscale events?

[05:24] Miguel Alvarez: good Q - our runtime manages KV cache migration across nodes during scaling. there's a short warmup period; we use sticky routing and pre-warmed standby instances for predictable tails. for workloads with high locality we can recommend a cache sizing + placement plan.

[05:40] Daniel Park: curious about quantization options - we use a quantized variant in prod to save cost. is that supported in dedicated? any tradeoffs on latency?

[05:48] Miguel Alvarez: yes we support quantized model variants. quantization often reduces memory and can slightly improve throughput but can impact absolute quality on some prompts; we recommend running an eval set during the benchmark to validate. sometimes int8 + kernel optimizations give the best cost/latency sweet spot.

[06:05] Samira Chen: pricing note - we'll send a matrix of base reserved pricing and burst/on-demand rates. many customers model two scenarios: steady-state reserved + 20-50% burst headroom.

[06:15] Priya Kapoor: for the pilot - will there be any PII touching logs outside our tenancy? we need to ensure tokens are not stored by default.

[06:22] Miguel Alvarez: by default we don't retain request payloads beyond what's necessary for debugging, and you can opt out of payload retention entirely for dedicated private deployments. we can include that in the security pack.

[06:33] Ethan Liu: integrations - we use Okta SAML for SSO; how's RBAC handled in the console?

[06:38] Samira Chen: we support SSO with SAML provisioning and fine-grained RBAC; you can map groups to roles and restrict access to audit logs and key management.

[06:47] Daniel Park: ok can you also outline failure modes? e.g., if a node dies during high burst, what's fallback behavior?

[06:53] Miguel Alvarez: we have multi-tier fallbacks: first we route to healthy instances within the pool; if capacity isn't available we can fall back to a compatible lower-cost model in a different pool or burst into on-demand capacity. for strict latency SLOs customers often keep a small standby headroom to avoid fallbacks.

[07:10] Priya Kapoor: we need all these fallback policies documented for our runbook.

[07:15] Samira Chen: we'll include a runbook example and recommended config for your p95 target.

[07:19] Daniel Park: timeline - we have an internal compliance gate on June 30th. if we want to pilot end-to-end before then, what's realistic?

[07:26] Miguel Alvarez: yes mid-June perf bench + 2-week pilot would fit before 6/30 if procurement moves quickly.

[07:32] Ethan Liu: what about model licensing - we currently use an open LLM with custom finetunes. do you support bringing our model artifacts? and does that change the security posture?

[07:41] Miguel Alvarez: you can bring your own model artifacts; we can host them in your dedicated pool. we require a model scan for known vulnerabilities but it doesn't materially change the tenancy model. for air-gapped on-prem private deployments we have a different process.

[07:54] Samira Chen: ok quick recap and next steps: we'll send SOC2 and security docs, pricing matrix for reserved + burst, and a proposed benchmark plan. miguel will own the benchmark plan and samira will own pricing + commercial. daniel/ethan to send sample traffic and eval prompts. Does that capture it?

[08:08] Daniel Park: yes, that's correct. i'll get the traffic profile and the p95 targets over by next week.

[08:14] Priya Kapoor: and we'll review SOC2 and kick off security Q&A once we receive the docs.

[08:19] Samira Chen: perfect. i'll follow up with the attachments and a calendar invite for the benchmark kickoff. thanks everyone.

[08:25] (end of call)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap and filler captured; some product names were transcribed slightly off (eg 'KV cache' rendered as 'kay vee cache' in a few places).
